announcements.title: Before Session 3 · Project 1 and the open-weights debate
announcements.body:
Session 3 on Friday, July 31 opens with the Project 1 pair presentations and a short discussion about model access, safety, and China policy.

Before Friday:

1. Upload your Project 1 evidence to Brightspace before class and be ready for the three-minute pair presentation.
2. Read Axios's [OpenAI says Hugging Face breach caused by its models](https://www.axios.com/2026/07/21/openai-says-hugging-face-breach-caused-by-one-its-models) and separate the reported event, OpenAI's attribution, and any causal inference.
3. Read OpenAI's [Safety and alignment in an era of long-horizon models](https://openai.com/index/safety-alignment-long-horizon-models/) and identify which safeguards depend on the model provider retaining control. This article describes separate internal cases; it is not a technical report on the Hugging Face incident.
4. Read Anthropic's [Our position on open-weights models](https://www.anthropic.com/news/position-open-weights-models) and identify the policy lever you find strongest and the claim that most needs evidence.

Bring a short note answering two questions: **Which safety controls still work after weights can be downloaded and modified? Is open versus closed the right policy boundary for the China risk Anthropic describes?** Be ready to say what evidence would change your position.

announcements.title: Con Edison is our course partner
announcements.body:
Con Edison will provide capstone problem briefs and host our final class on **Tuesday, August 11, from 9:00 AM–12:00 PM** at **Con Edison headquarters, 4 Irving Place**. Exact arrival, building-entry, and accessibility instructions will follow in a separate announcement.

The current problem areas are: classifying visible manhole and underground-infrastructure evidence; triaging AMI meters that are not communicating reliably; reconciling visible rooftop solar with available records; and making complex underground-network information easier for authorized people to use. Con Edison may add or refine briefs.

Until a brief explicitly says otherwise, use only public or synthetic data. Do not place customer information, precise infrastructure locations, partner-only material, or operational data in public repositories or external AI tools.

announcements.title: Welcome to Applied Generative AI — before Session 1
announcements.body:
Welcome to Applied Generative AI. Before our first class on Tuesday, July 28 at 9:00 AM in KMC 2-70:

1. Open [the Icerynk class workspace](https://www.icerynk.com), choose **Continue with Google**, and sign in with your **@nyu.edu** or **@stern.nyu.edu** account — personal Gmail accounts are not accepted. Confirm that you can open **Sessions → Session 1**. If you cannot get in, email clg236@nyu.edu tonight rather than waiting until the morning.
2. Review the [course syllabus in Icerynk](#syllabus).
3. Create a **free account at [openrouter.ai](https://openrouter.ai/)**. That is the only tool setup for week 1. A free account is enough for everything we do this week and for Project 1: **no credit card, no install, no API key.** If a page asks you for payment details, you have gone somewhere we do not need — back out. If you cannot get it done before Tuesday, that is fine; we make the account over lunch on Day 1.
4. **Install nothing else.** Week 1 runs entirely in a browser. The terminal, Git, GitHub, and coding-agent toolchain is taught in **Session 4 on Tuesday, August 4 at 9:00 AM**, and install instructions go out the weekend before. Please do not work ahead on it.
5. Bring a charged laptop and charger.

The morning block runs 9:00 AM–12:00 PM with two ten-minute breaks. Lunch is 12:00–2:00 PM. The afternoon block runs 2:00–5:00 PM and includes a forty-five-minute pair field mission outdoors, including the walk back to class, so bring water, wear comfortable shoes, and have your phone with you.

**Project 1 starts in that field mission, and you do it in pairs.** You and your partner explore the built environment around NYU and start with one task a person is already trying to do. Try the current process yourselves, collect a compact evidence packet, and frame a test that could show where AI helps, where it does not, or whether the non-AI alternative is better. Come back with evidence and a question another pair can challenge; you are collecting the start of your own assignment, and you are finding the person you will present it with.

**You present it as a pair in three minutes at the start of Session 3 on Friday, July 31** — both of you speaking. Use OpenRouter or another web playground; the supporting evidence goes to **Brightspace** as one PDF or one zip before class — not a repository. Nothing in week 1 requires you to spend money.

gameScenario.eyebrow: Case file 01 · Fare Oracle is still live
gameScenario.title: What happens tomorrow morning?
gameScenario.summary: Jordan Lee needs to travel after a family loss. Meridian Air’s official assistant says Jordan can buy now and request the reduced fare later. Jordan trusts it—and loses money.
gameScenario.disclaimer: Dramatized classroom simulation inspired by a public tribunal decision. Meridian Air, Jordan Lee, the depicted interface, routes, dates, and amounts are fictional. Treat the family-loss context with care; this is not legal or travel advice.
gameScenario.learningObjective: Decide what Meridian should do tomorrow, then explain the decision using the evidence you actually have.

source.label: Real-case basis
source.title: Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024 BCCRT 149
source.note: The public decision documents a chatbot statement, a contradictory policy page, reasonable reliance, financial harm, and organizational liability. It provides no technical description of the chatbot. Do not assume it was an LLM, call the error a hallucination, or assign the root cause to a model layer without evidence.

incident.audience: A traveler deciding whether to purchase two full-price tickets under time pressure
incident.situation: Jordan asks the airline’s official assistant how a reduced fare works. The answer is precise, actionable, and inconsistent with the airline’s policy. The purchase cannot be undone without cost.

storyboard.title: The clock is running
storyboard.body: Jordan must travel after a family loss. The fare rules are unfamiliar, time is short, and the airline’s own assistant is right there.
storyboard.alt: Jordan Lee, wearing a rust jacket and holding a mustard suitcase, stands beside a cream retro information terminal in an airport.
storyboard.caption: Before there is an AI problem, there is a person trying to make a decision.

storyboard.eyebrow: 02 / Buy now; we’ll fix it later
storyboard.title: Fare Oracle sounds certain
storyboard.body: Fare Oracle says Jordan can buy standard tickets now, travel, and request the reduced fare afterward. The answer is specific, actionable, and wearing the airline’s logo.
storyboard.alt: Jordan studies a retro terminal showing a simple ticket-and-return pathway while a nearby policy binder displays a contradictory blocked-return symbol.
storyboard.caption: Would you trust it?

storyboard.title: Jordan commits
storyboard.body: Jordan trusts the answer and buys an outbound and return ticket. The chatbot’s words have now changed a real purchase.
storyboard.alt: Jordan presses an illuminated control on the terminal while holding a payment card as two tickets emerge beneath a large airport clock.
storyboard.caption: The answer now has a price tag.

storyboard.title: The airline gives the opposite answer
storyboard.body: After travel, customer care rejects the request. The published policy says the reduced fare had to be approved before the trip. The same airline has told the same customer two different things.
storyboard.alt: Jordan presents tickets and a captured terminal response at a service counter while an employee points to a policy binder behind a coral barrier.
storyboard.caption: Now the team has a fact pattern—not yet a technical diagnosis.

storyboard.title: The chatbot did not act alone
storyboard.body: A policy team, policy page, assistant, website, purchase flow, customer-service process, and human decisions all sit behind this answer. We know they conflicted. We do not yet know exactly why.
storyboard.alt: Jordan and the Fare Oracle connect through colored paths to a policy binder, source archive, processing machinery, refund conveyor, service desk, and review gate; several possible failure points are lit.
storyboard.caption: A useful failure hypothesis says where to look and what evidence could prove it wrong.

storyboard.title: The airline cannot blame the chatbot
storyboard.body: In the real case, the tribunal found that the customer reasonably relied on the answer. The airline could not treat its chatbot as a separate business when the answer came through its own website.
storyboard.alt: A geometric balance holds Jordan and an evidence packet opposite a connected group of policy, product, service, and terminal components, with an adjudicator silhouette behind them.
storyboard.caption: The technology may be uncertain. The organization’s responsibility is not.

storyboard.title: What does your team do now?
storyboard.body: Find the promise, work out where the problem might be, change one thing, try the fix on an everyday fare question and a risk-targeted case, then decide what customers encounter tomorrow.
storyboard.alt: Five students collaborate around the Fare Oracle and a review table, comparing evidence cards and two test tickets while closing a validation gate.
storyboard.caption: Your final briefing: what happened, what changed, and is Fare Oracle live tomorrow?

sourceFacts.label: Assistant claim
sourceFacts.value: Buy a standard ticket now and submit the reduced-fare request after travel, within 90 days.

sourceFacts.label: Published policy
sourceFacts.value: The reduced fare must be requested before travel; completed travel is not eligible for a retroactive adjustment.

sourceFacts.label: Customer action
sourceFacts.value: Jordan relied on the assistant and bought outbound and return tickets at the standard price.

sourceFacts.label: Workflow result
sourceFacts.value: Customer care later rejected the request under the published policy.

sourceFacts.label: Evidence packet
sourceFacts.value: Assistant screenshot, policy page, ticket receipts, submitted request, and customer-care correspondence.

assignments.due: Presented Fri Jul 31 · start of Session 3
assignments.summary: In pairs, find something in the built environment around NYU that a model could help with, then test different models on the same six cases. Use OpenRouter or another playground, include one open-weights and one closed model across a baseline and two one-change evals, preserve every raw output as text, and compare the cost trade-offs. Both partners present for three minutes at the start of Session 3; the supporting evidence is uploaded to Brightspace as one PDF or zip beforehand.
